revenue: Open source and free to self-host: the pull request Action, the MCP server and the sandboxes run on the team's own Vultr account from scripts/up.sh, and the team pays Vultr for what it runs.
Hosted: a monthly subscription per protected database, with the control plane and sandboxes run for the team.
A support licence for regulated teams that self-host.
funnel: The pull request Action, rehearse only and free: every migration gets a comment saying what it really does.
MCP for the agent: it gives up its database URL, and every change waits for a person.
A short auto-apply list, once the team has seen enough reports.
next: Thin clones, so a rehearsal stays fast past a gigabyte, and masking personal data in the clone.
Clones restored from Vultr Managed PostgreSQL's own backups, so a rehearsal skips the dump.
An auto-apply list that grows: suggest additions from what a team keeps approving, and test each against the attacker first.
First customers: the free Action on real teams' migrations, listed on GitHub Marketplace, with its pull request comment pointing at the MCP setup; then paid protected databases.
A one-click deployment of infra/provision.py for the self-hosted tier, on the customer's own Vultr account.

competition.strength: Mature, fast, fit CI, and cover many databases. They check each change against a rule set and route it for approval.
competition.gap: A rule reads the statement. It doesn't measure what the plan really does to a full copy of your data.

competition.who: Thin clones and branches: DBLab, Neon
competition.strength: Far faster copies than our full restore. DBLab says about 10 seconds for 1 TiB.
competition.gap: A copy, not a decision: their docs describe no frozen guardrails or approval bound to a measured result. DBLab needs ZFS or LVM, and Neon's branches are on Neon.
safe-migrations-mcp simulates on prod in a rolled-back transaction, which still takes locks. DryRun uses sampled rows and only gives advice.

competition.who: A senior engineer reading the SQL
competition.strength: Knows what the business means, which no check encodes.
competition.gap: Has to guess what a statement cascades into, and doesn't scale with agents.

us.strength: A full clone in a no-network microVM, measured by Postgres. An approval bound to those exact hashes, and an apply that rolls back if prod differs.
us.weakness: Built for Postgres and Linux hosts. Rehearsals use full restores today, and thin clones are next, for databases past a gigabyte.
us.usp: An approval bound to the measured result of the exact plan, with an apply that rolls back if prod differs. None of the docs above describe that.
